definitions.definition: A rule that says the strength of something (like gravity or light) gets weaker as you move away from it, specifically by the square of the distance.
definitions.example: If you double your distance from a campfire, you get only one-quarter of the warmth.
definitions.first_appearance: The inverse-square law governed gravity for 13.8 billion years before Newton sat under a tree.

definitions.definition: A special number (about 1/137) that controls how strongly tiny particles like electrons interact with light and each other.
definitions.example: It's like a dial that sets how bright atoms glow and how strong chemical bonds are.
definitions.first_appearance: The fine structure constant (α ≈ 1/137) has been governing every atomic interaction since the first atoms formed

definitions.definition: The event about 13.8 billion years ago when the universe began expanding from an extremely hot, dense state.
definitions.example: Like a balloon inflating from a tiny point, but with space itself stretching out.
definitions.first_appearance: Big Bang. The laws of physics are already fully operative.

definitions.definition: The smallest possible unit of time, about 10⁻⁴³ seconds, after which our normal physics can start working.
definitions.example: It's like the first tick of the universe's clock, so short that a trillion trillion trillion of them fit in one second.
definitions.first_appearance: all 'set' from the first Planck time.

definitions.definition: The process where two small atomic nuclei smash together to form a bigger one, releasing huge amounts of energy.
definitions.example: This is what powers the sun and hydrogen bombs—like squeezing two ping-pong balls into one and getting a burst of heat.
definitions.first_appearance: Nuclear fusion begins, perfectly following E = mc².

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that describes how very tiny things like atoms and electrons behave, often in weird ways that differ from everyday objects.
definitions.example: It's like a set of rules for a microscopic world where particles can be in two places at once or spin both ways until you look at them.
definitions.first_appearance: Chemistry follows quantum mechanics.

definitions.definition: Einstein's famous equation that says energy (E) equals mass (m) times the speed of light (c) squared, meaning a tiny amount of mass can become a huge amount of energy.
definitions.example: This is why the sun shines: it turns a little bit of its mass into a lot of light and heat.
definitions.first_appearance: E = mc²

definitions.definition: Four mathematical rules that describe how electricity and magnetism work and how they create light and other electromagnetic waves.
definitions.example: These equations explain why a magnet can attract a paperclip and how radio waves travel from a tower to your phone.
definitions.first_appearance: Maxwell's equations described electromagnetic waves for the entire history of starlight before Maxwell formalized them in 1865.

definitions.definition: Waves of electric and magnetic energy that travel through space, including visible light, radio waves, X-rays, and microwaves.
definitions.example: Think of ripples in a pond, but instead of water, it's invisible fields of electricity and magnetism vibrating together.
definitions.first_appearance: Maxwell's equations described electromagnetic waves for the entire history of starlight before Maxwell formalized them in 1865.

definitions.definition: A fixed number that tells how strong gravity is between two objects based on their masses and distance apart.
definitions.example: It's like the 'strength knob' for gravity—if it were different, planets might not orbit stars properly.
definitions.first_appearance: The fine structure constant, gravitational constant, speed of light — all 'set' from the first Planck time.

definitions.definition: The fastest possible speed in the universe, about 300,000 kilometers per second (186,000 miles per second), at which light and all electromagnetic waves travel.
definitions.example: It's so fast that light from the sun reaches Earth in about 8 minutes, but it's still a limit—nothing can go faster.
definitions.first_appearance: The fine structure constant, gravitational constant, speed of light — all 'set' from the first Planck time.

definitions.definition: Not made of physical stuff; existing without a body or substance you can touch.
definitions.example: Thoughts and numbers are immaterial—you can't weigh them or hold them, but they are real.
definitions.first_appearance: This substrate is necessarily immaterial (not in matter)

definitions.definition: Existing forever, without beginning or end; outside of time.
definitions.example: If something is eternal, it never started and will never stop—like the number 2, which has always been true.
definitions.first_appearance: necessarily eternal (predates everything)

definitions.definition: Based on logic and reason; orderly and understandable by thinking.
definitions.example: A rational explanation makes sense step by step, like solving a puzzle with clear rules.
definitions.first_appearance: necessarily rational (it IS the mathematical order)

definitions.definition: The underlying layer or foundation that something else rests on or comes from.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for plants—it's what supports and feeds them.
definitions.first_appearance: exists in a substrate that precedes matter

definitions.definition: To put something into a clear, structured, written form using rules and definitions.
definitions.example: When you write down the rules of a game so everyone knows them, you formalize the game.
definitions.first_appearance: Euclid formalizes geometry.

definitions.definition: A Greek word (pronounced 'LOH-gos') meaning 'word,' 'reason,' 'order,' or 'logic'—the principle of rational structure in the universe.
definitions.example: In ancient Greek philosophy, Logos was the force that made the cosmos orderly, like a blueprint for reality.
definitions.first_appearance: John 1:1 says: 'In the beginning was the Logos.'

definitions.definition: The ability to cause something to happen or to affect other things.
definitions.example: A rock has causal power because it can break a window; a thought has causal power because it can make you act.
definitions.first_appearance: If the math exists 'nowhere,' then it has no causal power.

definitions.definition: Working or in effect; actively doing its job.
definitions.example: The rules of a game are operative from the moment you start playing.
definitions.first_appearance: The math was operative the entire time.

definitions.definition: The part of the universe we can see from Earth, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang (about 93 billion light-years across).
definitions.example: It's like a bubble around us—we can't see beyond it because light from farther away hasn't reached us yet.
definitions.first_appearance: The equation was already governing nuclear fusion in every star in the observable universe.

definitions.definition: The scientific name for the human species, meaning 'wise person' in Latin.
definitions.example: All modern humans belong to the species Homo sapiens.
definitions.first_appearance: Homo sapiens appears.

definitions.definition: Short for 'Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica,' Isaac Newton's famous book that laid out the laws of motion and gravity.
definitions.example: It's like the instruction manual for how planets move and apples fall.
definitions.first_appearance: Newton publishes the Principia.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that says the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at constant speed, and that the speed of light is always the same no matter how fast you go.
definitions.example: It explains why time slows down for things moving very fast, like in sci-fi movies where astronauts age slower.
definitions.first_appearance: Einstein publishes Special Relativity.

stats.highest_grade_level: Planck time (grade 12), fine structure constant (grade 12), Maxwell's equations (grade 12), Logos (grade 12), Special Relativity (grade 12)
